question: Who can freeze, burn or block a stablecoin?
answer: For 18 of the 36 crypto dollars here, the issuer can freeze or block coins, usually for suspected crime or on a court or government order. The GENIUS Act requires payment-stablecoin issuers to be able to do this.

items.title: Freeze, burn or block
items.text: A 'lawful order' is one that requires a person to seize, freeze, burn or prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins it issued. A permitted issuer may issue only if it has the technical ability to comply with such orders. A foreign issuer's coin may be offered in the U.S. only if the issuer can and will comply with lawful orders.
kv: requires a person to seize, freeze, burn, or prevent the transfer of payment stablecoins issued by the person (Sec. 2(16)(A))

catalog_context.title: What makes a legal stablecoin trustworthy
catalog_context.answer: Under the GENIUS Act there is no single stamp that makes a stablecoin "trusted": the issuer's approval, the coin's code and keys, its reserves, the platforms selling it and the fixes for mistakes each have to be proven separately.

catalog_context.title: OCC final stablecoin rules: issuer duties, permissions and operating evidence
catalog_context.answer: The OCC's final GENIUS rule takes effect January 18, 2027. Its requirements attach to specific issuers, claims and custody relationships; approval, backing, capital, reporting and completed redemption require separate evidence.
